sets.title: Urban Beekeeping
text: Over the past decade, keeping bees on city rooftops {{1}} become a surprisingly popular hobby. What began as a niche pursuit among a handful of enthusiasts has turned {{2}} a genuine urban movement, with hives now appearing on office blocks, hotels and even hospital roofs.

Supporters argue that urban beekeeping helps pollinate parks and gardens, {{3}} in turn supports a wider range of plant and insect life across the city. Critics, {{4}}, point out that cities may simply not have enough flowers to support so many hives, {{5}} that an excess of honeybees could end up competing with wild bees and other pollinators for the same limited food.

{{6}} matter how well intentioned, a rooftop hive is not something to take on lightly: bees require regular inspection, and a swarm {{7}} escapes above a busy street can cause genuine alarm. Even so, {{8}} the right training and support, most new beekeepers manage perfectly well, and many say the hobby has reconnected them with the changing seasons in a city that often feels disconnected from nature.

questions.explanation: The present perfect ('has become') is needed because the sentence describes a change that started in the past and is still true now ('over the past decade').
'Turn into' is the fixed phrasal verb meaning 'change or develop into something'.
'Which' is needed to introduce a non-restrictive relative clause referring back to the whole idea of helping pollinate parks and gardens.
'However' marks the contrast between the supporters' view in the previous sentence and the critics' concern here.
'And' links two parallel 'that'-clauses after 'point out', joining the two reasons the critics give.
'No matter how' is the fixed phrase meaning 'regardless of how'.
A subject relative pronoun referring to 'a swarm' is needed; both 'that' and 'which' are acceptable here.
'With the right training and support' means 'provided that they have'; 'with' introduces the accompanying condition.

sets.title: The Art of Negotiation
text: Good negotiators are often assumed to be born {{1}} natural persuasive instincts, but research suggests that negotiation is, in fact, a skill {{2}} can be learned and refined like any other. Experienced negotiators prepare thoroughly, gather information about the other side, and resist the temptation to reveal their own position too early.

One common mistake is to focus too {{3}} on price alone, {{4}} ignoring other factors that might matter just as much to the other party, such as timing, flexibility or long-term trust. Skilled negotiators instead look {{5}} ways to expand the overall deal, so that both sides can walk away feeling they gained something.

{{6}} the negotiation becomes tense, experienced negotiators rarely raise their voice or walk out; {{7}} they tend to pause, ask clarifying questions, and give the other side room to reconsider. It is this calm persistence, {{8}} than aggressive pressure, that most consistently produces lasting agreements, and it is a quality that can be practised deliberately long before anyone sits down at the table.

questions.explanation: 'Born with' is the fixed phrase for having a quality from birth.
A subject relative pronoun referring to 'a skill' is needed; 'that' or 'which' both work.
'Focus too much on' is the natural quantifying collocation describing excessive attention.
A linking adverb meaning 'as a result' is needed before the participle 'ignoring'; 'thereby' and 'thus' both fit.
'Look for ways' is the fixed phrasal pattern meaning 'try to find ways'.
'When' or 'if' can both introduce the condition/time under which negotiators behave calmly.
'Instead' or 'rather' both contrast what experienced negotiators do not do (raise their voice) with what they do instead (pause and ask questions).
'Rather than' is the fixed comparative phrase contrasting calm persistence with aggressive pressure.

sets.title: Space Tourism
text: For most of the twentieth century, space travel {{1}} something only trained astronauts could even dream of attempting. Today, a handful of private companies are racing to make short trips beyond the atmosphere available to anyone {{2}} can afford the ticket.

Early flights have lasted only a few minutes, giving passengers {{3}} enough time to experience weightlessness before the capsule begins its descent. Even so, demand has been strong: {{4}} the eye-watering prices, thousands of people have already registered their interest for future flights.

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Environmental campaigners warn that each flight burns through a disproportionate amount of fuel for the number of passengers carried, and argue that the industry should be regulated far more {{5}} than it currently is. Supporters counter {{6}} pointing out that the technology developed for tourism often filters down into cheaper, more efficient launch systems, so {{7}} everyone eventually benefits.
{{8}} far this remains a niche market reserved for the very wealthy, but few doubt that prices will fall as competition between companies increases.

questions.explanation: The past simple is needed because the sentence describes the whole of the twentieth century as a finished historical period.
'Who' introduces a relative clause referring back to the person 'anyone'.
'Just enough time' emphasises that the amount of time was the bare minimum needed.
'Despite' introduces a noun phrase ('the eye-watering prices') that contrasts with the strong demand described.
An adverb meaning 'with stricter control' is needed after 'more'; 'closely', 'tightly' and 'strictly' are all natural collocations with 'regulated'.
'Counter by doing something' is the fixed pattern for describing how someone responds to an argument.
'So that' is the fixed purpose/result structure; 'so' is already given, so the gap needs 'that' to complete it before the result clause 'everyone eventually benefits'.
'So far' and 'thus far' are both fixed phrases meaning 'up to now'.

sets.title: The Decline of Handwriting
text: Fewer and fewer adults now write anything by hand beyond signing their name, and in {{1}} schools, typing is taught alongside, or even instead {{2}}, handwriting. Some educators welcome the change, arguing that keyboard skills matter {{3}} in a digital world than the ability to form neat letters with a pen.

Others are far {{4}} convinced. Studies suggest that the physical act of writing by hand engages the brain differently from typing, helping students remember {{5}} they have written more effectively than if they had simply typed it. {{6}} this research is far from conclusive, it has been enough to persuade several countries to keep handwriting lessons compulsory in primary schools.

Whatever the eventual outcome, few believe that handwriting will disappear {{7}}: even committed typists still reach for a pen to jot down a quick note or sign a card, {{8}} the keyboard is nowhere in sight. For most people, it seems, the debate is less about choosing sides than about finding room for both skills in a world that increasingly demands speed as well as thought.

questions.explanation: A quantifier describing a general but not total number of schools is needed; 'many', 'some' and 'most' all work naturally here.
'Instead of' is the fixed phrase meaning 'in place of'.
'Matter more... than' is the comparative structure needed to contrast the importance of the two skills.
'Far less convinced' and 'far from convinced' are both fixed ways of showing the opposite degree of conviction from the educators who welcome the change.
'What they have written' is the noun clause object of 'remember'; 'what' is needed because there is no specific antecedent.
A concessive linker is needed to contrast the inconclusive research with its real-world influence; 'while', 'although' and 'though' all fit.
An adverb meaning 'completely' is needed after 'disappear'; 'altogether', 'entirely' and 'completely' are all acceptable here.
A linker introducing the circumstance in which people still reach for a pen is needed; 'when', 'while' and 'if' all fit this meaning.
